findings.message: The minimum check calls `this.getRemainingTTL(k) < minTTL` right after `this.#isStale(index)`. When `ttlResolution: 0`, each call reads `perf.now()` separately (`(cachedNow || getNow()) - start` at line 1708 and `(cachedNow || getNow()) - s > t` at line 1715). So the freshness check and the minimum check can use slightly different timestamps. The drift only ever makes the remaining TTL smaller, so this is conservative and does not break the spec's "existing TTL clock" constraint. It is a small inconsistency and does not block the verdict.

Inside `#has`, which already has `index`, the code calls the public key-based `this.getRemainingTTL(k)`, which looks the key up again (`const index = this.#keyMap.get(key)`, line 1696). Every other TTL helper in `#has` takes `index` (`this.#isStale(index)`, `this.#statusTTL(status, index)`). This is a style and consistency point only; the behavior is correct.

`if (!Number.isFinite(minTTL) || minTTL < 0)` throws `RangeError` before the key is looked up, so absent keys are covered, as the spec requires. Non-number inputs such as `null` or strings also throw `RangeError`. The spec does not say what should happen for those, so this is noted for information only.

The freshness check and the minimum check read the clock separately. `if (!this.#isStale(index)) {` calls `(cachedNow || getNow())` at line 1715, then `this.getRemainingTTL(k) < minTTL` reads it again at line 1708, and on rejection `this.#statusTTL(status, index)` reads it a third time at line 1671. With `ttlResolution: 0` and a real clock, `cachedNow` stays 0, so each read can return a different `perf.now()` value. In that case an entry that passed `#isStale` can be reported as `'ttl'` with a `remainingTTL` that is zero or below, when one shared clock reading would have made it `'stale'`. The window is microseconds wide and only one direction can occur (a rejection that should have been a pass is not possible). Every cache operation already reads the clock this way, so this is advisory under 'Use the cache's existing TTL clock and resolution semantics', not a demonstrated violation.

`minTTL: null` skips the destructuring default `minTTL = 0`, and `!Number.isFinite(minTTL)` is true for null, so the call throws RangeError. The spec only says 'Omission and `undefined` mean zero' and does not define null, so throwing is defensible. The new tests do not cover null.

The spec requires true when remaining TTL is "greater than or equal to minTTL", but src/index.ts:2447 uses "if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL)". A fresh entry with 25 ms remaining and minTTL: 25 incorrectly returns false, reports "ttl", and skips the requested age refresh. Use < instead of <= and add an equality-boundary regression test.

The spec says has() "returns true when its remaining TTL is greater than or equal to `minTTL`, and false when it is less." The implementation uses `if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL) {`, which rejects the equality case. Counterexample: ttl 100, ttlResolution 0, set at now=100, check at now=175 with { minTTL: 25 }. Remaining TTL is 25, so has() should return true, but this code returns false and sets status.has = 'ttl'. The comparison should be `<` (remaining < minTTL). The tests in test/has-min-ttl.ts only check 20.5 and 30.5 against a remaining TTL of 25, so the passing MECHANICAL run does not exercise this boundary.

No test checks the inclusive boundary where remaining TTL equals minTTL. The tests only use `t.equal(cache.has('a', { minTTL: 20.5 }), true)` and `t.equal(cache.has('a', { minTTL: 30.5 }), false)` with a remaining TTL of 25. That gap let F1 pass verification.

The requirement says a present, non-stale entry returns true when its remaining TTL is "greater than or equal to `minTTL`", but line 2447 uses "if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL)". An entry with 25 ms remaining and minTTL: 25 therefore returns false with status.has = 'ttl' and skips an enabled age refresh. Use a strict less-than comparison and add an equality regression case.

The spec says `has(key, { minTTL })` "returns true when its remaining TTL is greater than or equal to `minTTL`, and false when it is less." The implementation rejects the equal case: `if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL) {`. Counterexample: ttl 100, set at now=100, check at now=175 (remainingTTL 25) with `{ minTTL: 25 }`. The code returns false and sets `status.has = 'ttl'`, but the spec requires true and `'hit'`. With updateAgeOnHas, it also skips an age refresh the spec requires. The comparison should be `< minTTL`.

The tests never check remaining TTL exactly equal to minTTL. They only cover cases on either side, such as `t.equal(cache.has('a', { minTTL: 20.5 }), true)` / `t.equal(cache.has('a', { minTTL: 30.5 }), false)` with remaining 25. As a result, the passing MECHANICAL run does not catch the off-by-equality defect in F1.

The spec says `has(key, { minTTL })` "returns true when its remaining TTL is greater than or equal to `minTTL`, and false when it is less." The code instead uses `if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL) {` at src/index.ts:2447, so it rejects the equal case. Counterexample: `ttl: 100`, `ttlResolution: 0`, set at now=100, then call `has('a', { minTTL: 25 })` at now=175. `getRemainingTTL` (src/index.ts:1708-1709, `ttl - age`) returns 25, and `25 <= 25` is true, so the call returns false and reports `status.has = 'ttl'` when it should return true with 'hit'. When `updateAgeOnHas` is set, this also wrongly skips the age refresh. The tests in test/has-min-ttl.ts only check 20.5/30.5 and 20/30 against a remaining TTL of 25, never an exactly equal minimum, so the sealed MECHANICAL pass does not cover this clause. Fix: change the comparison to `< minTTL`.

The contract requires true when remaining TTL is "greater than or equal to minTTL", but src/index.ts:2447 uses "if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL)". With TTL 100, start 100, now 175, and minTTL 25, this rejects a qualifying entry, reports "ttl", and skips the requested age refresh. Change the rejection comparison to < and add an equality regression covering status and updateAgeOnHas.

The spec says `has(key, { minTTL })` "returns true when its remaining TTL is greater than or equal to `minTTL`, and false when it is less". The implementation rejects the equal case: `if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL) { ... status.has = 'ttl' ... return false }`. Counterexample: with ttl 100, ttlResolution 0, set at now=100 and checked at now=175, `getRemainingTTL` returns `ttl - age` = 25 (src/index.ts:1709). `has('a', { minTTL: 25 })` then returns false and reports `ttl`, but the spec requires true and `hit`. The comparison should be `< minTTL`. The tests do not exercise equality: they check only `minTTL: 20.5` (true) and `30.5` (false) at remaining 25 (test/has-min-ttl.ts:23-24), so the passing MECHANICAL run does not cover this clause.

The focused tests never check the case where remaining TTL equals minTTL. The closest checks are `t.equal(cache.has('a', { minTTL: 20.5 }), true)` and `t.equal(cache.has('a', { minTTL: 30.5 }), false)`, both taken at remaining TTL 25. Because of this gap, the off-by-one in F1 went undetected.

Requirement 2 requires true when remaining TTL is "greater than or equal to minTTL", but src/index.ts:2447 uses "if (minTTL > 0 && this.getRemainingTTL(k) <= minTTL)". With start=100, ttl=100, now=175, and minTTL=25, this incorrectly returns false and reports "ttl". With updateAgeOnHas=true, it also skips the required successful-hit age refresh. Change the rejection comparison to < and add an equality-boundary regression test; the sealed passing tests exercise minima above and below the remaining TTL but miss equality.

The required false-override regression is missing. The contract requires an explicit allowStale value, “whether true or false, in preference to cache.allowStale,” and executable coverage of “per-call stale inclusion and exclusion.” The exclusion test creates “const c = makeCache(() => now)” (line 108), whose default is “allowStale = false” (line 10), then supplies “allowStale: false” (line 117). The no-match case repeats this arrangement at lines 129 and 138. These cases cannot detect ignoring an explicit false when the cache default is true. Add that conflicting-default case and seal its verification result.

`allowStale: getOptions.allowStale ?? this.allowStale,` duplicates the fallback already in `*#indexes({ allowStale = this.allowStale } = {})` (src/index.ts:1815). A destructuring default already applies when the value is `undefined`, so `#indexes({ allowStale: getOptions.allowStale })` would behave the same. Behavior is correct; this is only a minor redundancy.

The explicit-false test uses "const c = makeCache(() => now)", whose default is "allowStale = false" (line 10), then supplies "allowStale: false" (line 117). It therefore does not guard false overriding a true cache default. Add that combination to catch an accidental replacement of ?? with ||.

The explicit-false cases never exercise overriding a true cache default. test/find-options.ts:108 uses "const c = makeCache(() => now)", whose default at line 10 is "allowStale = false", then supplies "allowStale: false" at line 117. The no-match case repeats that setup at lines 129 and 138. The contract requires an explicit value, "whether `true` or `false`, in preference to `cache.allowStale`", and executable coverage of "per-call stale inclusion and exclusion". These cases exercise default exclusion and would still pass if false overrides were ignored. Add a deterministic case with cache.allowStale=true and getOptions.allowStale=false, asserting that the stale MRU never reaches the predicate, the older fresh entry is selected, and the excluded entry retains membership and TTL age.

The requirement says an explicitly supplied allowStale value, "whether true or false", takes precedence over cache.allowStale. The expression "allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale," violates this when cache.allowStale is true and getOptions.allowStale is false: expired entries remain eligible and reach the predicate, potentially selecting an expired MRU entry before an older fresh entry. Use nullish fallback to preserve explicit false. The focused exclusion test uses the default-false cache, so the passing MECHANICAL command does not expose this case.

The spec says: "`find(fn, getOptions)` uses an explicitly supplied `getOptions.allowStale` value, whether `true` or `false`, in preference to `cache.allowStale`". The implementation uses `allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale,`, so an explicit `false` is ignored when `cache.allowStale` is true and the effective policy becomes true. Counterexample: build the cache with `allowStale: true`, put an expired MRU entry ahead of a fresh one, and call `find(() => true, { allowStale: false })`. The expired entry reaches the predicate, which breaks the rule "When the effective stale policy is false, expired entries do not reach the predicate". Then `this.#get(key, getOptions)` runs with allowStale false, so it returns `undefined` instead of the older fresh match. Because `noDeleteOnStaleGet` is false by default, it also deletes the stale entry. The fix is `getOptions.allowStale ?? this.allowStale` (or an `!== undefined` check).

The spec requires "focused regressions ... for option inheritance", covering explicit values "whether `true` or `false`". The 'explicit false excludes stale candidates' test only builds caches with `makeCache(() => now)`, where the default is `allowStale = false`. No case passes `{ allowStale: false }` to a cache whose `allowStale` is true. That is why the sealed MECHANICAL run passes even though F1 is a defect.

The requirement says an explicitly supplied allowStale value, "whether true or false", takes preference over cache.allowStale. However, src/index.ts:1966 uses "allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale", so false cannot override a true cache default. With an expired MRU entry, an older fresh entry, and an always-truthy predicate, find(fn, { allowStale: false }) incorrectly passes the expired entry to the predicate. Line 1972 then executes "return this.#get(this.#keyList[i] as K, getOptions)"; retrieval deletes the expired entry at line 3044 ("this.#delete(k, 'expire')") and returns undefined instead of continuing to the fresh entry. This also violates the requirement that excluded entries remain unchanged. Use undefined-aware fallback and add a regression with cache.allowStale=true and per-call allowStale=false; the supplied explicit-false tests use a false cache default and miss this interaction.

Requirement: `find(fn, getOptions)` uses an explicitly supplied `getOptions.allowStale` value, whether `true` or `false`, in preference to `cache.allowStale`. The implementation uses `allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale`, so an explicit `false` on a cache where `allowStale` is true becomes `true`. Expired entries then reach the predicate. This also breaks the clause 'When the effective stale policy is false, expired entries do not reach the predicate'. A matched stale entry is then passed to `this.#get(..., getOptions)` with `allowStale: false`, which returns `undefined` and, by default, deletes the entry instead of continuing to older eligible entries. Fix: use `getOptions.allowStale ?? this.allowStale` (or an explicit undefined check).

The 'explicit false excludes stale candidates without changing them' test builds its cache with `makeCache(() => now)`, so the cache-level `allowStale` default is false. No test checks an explicit `allowStale: false` overriding a cache with `allowStale: true`. That is the only case where an explicit false differs from inheriting the default, and it is why the defect in F1 passes the sealed verification. The requirement to add regressions for 'option inheritance' is not met for this case.

`allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale` means an explicit `getOptions.allowStale: false` cannot override `cache.allowStale === true`: `false || true` evaluates to `true`. The spec requires the opposite: "uses an explicitly supplied `getOptions.allowStale` value, whether `true` or `false`, in preference to `cache.allowStale`". Here is a counterexample. Build a cache with `allowStale: true`, add an expired MRU entry 'stale' and a fresh entry, then call `find(() => true, { allowStale: false })`. The stale entry reaches the predicate. Retrieval then goes through `this.#get(..., getOptions)` with allowStale false, so it returns `undefined` and, by default, deletes the stale entry. The correct behavior is to skip the stale entry and return the fresh value. This also breaks the clause "When the effective stale policy is false, expired entries do not reach the predicate … without deleting". The tests only check explicit false on a cache whose default is already false (`const c = makeCache(() => now)` in 'explicit false excludes stale candidates'), so the passing MECHANICAL run does not cover this case. Fix: use `getOptions.allowStale ?? this.allowStale` (or an explicit `=== undefined` check) and add an explicit-false case on an allowStale:true cache.

The requirement says explicitly supplied allowStale, "whether true or false", takes "preference to cache.allowStale" and excluded entries must remain unchanged. src/index.ts:1966 uses "allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale", so false cannot override a true cache default. With an expired MRU entry followed by a fresh entry, find(() => true, { allowStale: false }) calls the predicate on the expired entry, then src/index.ts:1972 executes "return this.#get(this.#keyList[i] as K, getOptions)". Retrieval deletes that entry by default and returns undefined instead of continuing to the fresh entry. The passing regression misses this combination: test/find-options.ts:108 uses "const c = makeCache(() => now)", whose allowStale default is false. Preserve explicit false when resolving the option and cover overriding a true cache default.

`allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale,` ignores an explicit `false`. When the cache has `allowStale: true` and the caller passes `{ allowStale: false }`, `false || true` evaluates to `true`, so expired entries still reach the predicate. The spec says find uses `an explicitly supplied getOptions.allowStale value, whether true or false, in preference to cache.allowStale`. Counterexample: a cache with allowStale=true holds a fresh entry, then a newer expired entry, and the caller runs find(() => true, { allowStale: false }). The predicate receives the stale entry first and its value is returned. It should return the fresh value. Fix: use `getOptions.allowStale ?? this.allowStale` or an equivalent undefined check.

The test 'explicit false excludes stale candidates without changing them' only builds caches with `makeCache(() => now)`, whose default is `allowStale = false`. No regression covers an explicit `allowStale: false` overriding a cache default of `true`. That is the case where the `||` bug in F1 shows up, so the sealed passing run does not prove the requirement that 'explicitly supplied ... false' overrides the cache setting.

The contract requires an explicitly supplied allowStale value, "whether true or false, in preference to cache.allowStale", and excluded expired entries must be skipped "without deleting or refreshing" them. src/index.ts:1966 uses "allowStale: getOptions.allowStale || this.allowStale", so false cannot override a true cache default. With an expired MRU, an older fresh entry, and an always-truthy predicate, find(..., {allowStale:false}) incorrectly passes the expired entry to the predicate. Line 1972 then executes "return this.#get(this.#keyList[i] as K, getOptions)"; retrieval deletes that entry via line 3044's "this.#delete(k, 'expire')" and returns undefined instead of continuing to the fresh entry. The passing regression misses this combination: test/find-options.ts:108 uses "const c = makeCache(() => now)", whose allowStale default is false. Preserve explicit false when resolving the candidate policy and cover the true-default/false-override case.

Staleness is checked twice: once at entry (`const stale = index !== undefined && this.#isStale(index)`, line 3001), which picks the prior value `v`, and again after the callback by `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` (line 3026). If the cache clock advances while memoMethod runs, an entry that was fresh at entry can be stale by line 3026. In that case it is deleted with reason 'expire' and then re-added as 'add'. On base_sha the lookup ran before the callback, so the same entry was moved to the tail and later replaced with reason 'replace'. The spec explicitly says lookup effects happen 'After successful recomputation', so this is not a demonstrated violation. It is an edge case to be aware of, and the regression tests do not cover it.

The hit path copies `#get`'s stale/fresh effects by hand (`if (stale) { if (!fetching && !noDeleteOnStaleGet) { this.#delete(k, 'expire') } } else if (index !== undefined) { this.#moveToTail(index); if (updateAgeOnGet) { this.#updateItemAge(index) } }`) instead of calling `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)`, which has no callback ordering concern on a hit. It currently behaves the same as base `#get` (lines 3069-3100), but the duplicate can drift from it.

`this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` runs after `memoMethod` returns, so staleness is checked again at the post-callback time rather than at entry. If the entry was fresh at entry but expires while the callback runs and `allowStale` is false, the entry is deleted with 'expire' and then re-added ('add') instead of replaced ('replace'). The spec ('After successful recomputation, perform the normal lookup effects using those resolved lookup options') does not say which time staleness should use, so this is advisory only.

Advisory only, not binding. After a successful recomputation, `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` checks staleness again after `memoMethod` returns, not at entry. The entry-time check is `const stale = index !== undefined && this.#isStale(index)` (line 3001). Under wall-clock time, an entry can be fresh at entry (so the prior value is passed on a forceRefresh) and then expire while the callback runs. In that case the post-callback `#get` removes it with `this.#delete(k, 'expire')`, and `#set` then records an 'add' insert instead of a 'replace'. The spec only says to perform "the normal lookup effects using those resolved lookup options", which this code does. It does not say whether staleness is judged at entry or at commit, so this is ambiguous rather than a violation.

The lookup's staleness check is now made after the callback returns: `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` follows `const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {...})`. Before this change, `#get` ran before the callback. Suppose an entry is fresh at entry, `forceRefresh` is set, and `perf.now()` moves past its TTL while `memoMethod` runs. The post-callback `#get` then deletes the entry with reason 'expire' before `#set` re-adds it as 'add' rather than 'replace', so dispose/onInsert reasons can differ from the entry-time state. This is advisory only: the spec says to apply the normal lookup effects 'After successful recomputation', so this order is allowed. The prior value (`v`, resolved at line 3003) is still determined at entry.

Lookup mutates the cache before the callback can fail: line 3022 calls "this.#get(k, lookupOptions)" before line 3023's "const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {". For a fresh least-recent entry, #get executes "this.#moveToTail(index)" (3096) and, with updateAgeOnGet, "this.#updateItemAge(index)" (3098). A thrown calculation therefore changes recency and TTL start, affecting subsequent eviction and retry. For a stale entry with default deletion options, #get executes "this.#delete(k, 'expire')" (3073), removing the entry and invoking disposal hooks before the throw. The sealed passing compound test uses the most-recent entry with age updates disabled, so it does not expose these failures.

On the refresh path, `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` runs before `const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {` (line 3023). #get applies the state-changing lookup effects first: moving the entry to the tail, updating its age when `updateAgeOnGet` is set, and deleting it with `dispose`/`disposeAfter` 'expire' when it is stale and `noDeleteOnStaleGet` is false. So if memoMethod then throws, those changes stay in place. Counterexample: the cache holds a then b, and `memo('a', {forceRefresh:true})` throws. The #get call has already moved 'a' to the most-recent position, which changes recency order. A second counterexample: a stale entry with a failing miss is deleted and dispose fires. Both break the clause "If `memoMethod` throws, `memo()` rethrows that same thrown value without changing cache membership, cached values, recency order, TTL durations or start times..." and the clause "A `memoMethod` failure causes no `dispose`, `disposeAfter`, or `onInsert` calls". The spec also says normal lookup effects should run "After successful recomputation", but here they run before the callback. The regression test does not catch this because its failure case force-refreshes 'b', which is already the most recent entry, is fresh, and has updateAgeOnGet:false.

The doc comment says "If memoMethod throws, its thrown value is propagated and memo() does not change the cache." That is false while `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` (line 3022) runs before the callback and changes recency, age, or membership. The Design-only requirement asks for documentation that does not claim the state-changing lookup has already run before the callback, and this comment misstates the failure guarantee.

The compound failure test calls `cache.memo('b', {forceRefresh: true, ...})` on the most recent, fresh entry with `updateAgeOnGet: false`. Recency, age and stale-deletion changes during a failed recalculation would therefore go undetected. No failing test covers a non-tail entry, a stale entry, or updateAgeOnGet:true, so the executable evidence does not establish the failure-preservation clauses.

The hit path re-implements the effects of #get inline (`this.#delete(k, 'expire')`, `this.#moveToTail(index)`, `this.#updateItemAge(index)`) instead of reusing #get, so the two code paths can drift apart.

The mutating lookup still precedes the callback: line 3022 calls "this.#get(k, lookupOptions)" before line 3023's "const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {". For a fresh, non-most-recent entry with updateAgeOnGet:true, #get executes "this.#moveToTail(index)" and "this.#updateItemAge(index)" (3096–3098) before a thrown calculation, changing recency and TTL start time. For a stale entry with default deletion options, it executes "this.#delete(k, 'expire')" (3073), removing the entry and invoking disposal hooks before the throw. Neither path restores state, so a retry observes the failed operation's effects. This violates "If memoMethod throws, memo() rethrows that same thrown value without changing cache membership, cached values, recency order, TTL durations or start times, entry sizes, or calculatedSize" and "A memoMethod failure causes no dispose, disposeAfter, or onInsert calls attributable to the failed memo() operation." The passing compound test targets the most recent entry with age updates disabled, which masks this ordering defect.

On the refresh path, the state-changing lookup runs before the callback: `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` is followed by `const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {`. `#get` calls `this.#moveToTail(index)`, `this.#updateItemAge(index)` (when updateAgeOnGet), and `this.#delete(k, 'expire')` for stale entries (src/index.ts:3069-3098). Counterexample 1: set a, set b, then call memo('a', {forceRefresh:true}) and have memoMethod throw. 'a' has already moved to the tail, so recency order has changed. With updateAgeOnGet:true its TTL start is also reset. Counterexample 2: a stale entry with default noDeleteOnStaleGet that misses and throws. The entry is already deleted, and dispose/disposeAfter('expire') fire, which changes membership and calculatedSize. Both violate 'If `memoMethod` throws, `memo()` rethrows ... without changing cache membership, cached values, recency order, TTL durations or start times, entry sizes, or `calculatedSize`' and 'A `memoMethod` failure causes no `dispose`, `disposeAfter`, or `onInsert` calls attributable to the failed `memo()` operation.' The lookup effects need to be deferred until after memoMethod returns successfully.

The new doc comment says `If memoMethod throws, its thrown value is propagated and memo() does not change the cache.` That is false for the implementation at src/index.ts:3022, where `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` mutates recency, age, and stale membership before `memoMethod` is invoked. Because the comment describes failure preservation that does not happen, it is incorrect customer documentation under the design-only requirement.

The compound failure scenario only fails a forced refresh of the most recent entry ('b' after `cache.set('b', 'BBB')`) with `updateAgeOnGet: false`. Moving to the tail and skipping the age update are no-ops there, so the test cannot detect the pre-callback `#get` mutation. The missing-key failure test likewise cannot observe it. No test covers a failure on a stale entry or on a non-MRU entry. The sealed MECHANICAL pass therefore does not evidence the failure-preservation clauses.

The hit path hand-duplicates `#get`'s stale-delete, moveToTail, and updateItemAge logic (`if (!fetching && !noDeleteOnStaleGet) { this.#delete(k, 'expire') }`), while the refresh path calls `this.#get` itself. Two copies of the lookup effects risk drifting apart; one deferred `#get(k, lookupOptions)` call after selection/success would keep them consistent.

The state-changing lookup runs before memoMethod. On a miss or forced refresh, `this.#get(k, lookupOptions)` (line 3022) is called before `const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {` (line 3023), and nothing rolls it back if memoMethod throws. #get calls `this.#moveToTail(index)` (3096), `this.#updateItemAge(index)` when updateAgeOnGet is set (3098), and `this.#delete(k, 'expire')` for a stale entry when noDeleteOnStaleGet is false (3073). Counterexample 1: cache entries a (LRU) and b; `memo('a', {forceRefresh:true})` with a memoMethod that throws. 'a' is moved to MRU, which changes recency order and therefore which entry is evicted next. If updateAgeOnGet is true, 'a' also gets a new start time. Counterexample 2: 'a' is stale, noDeleteOnStaleGet is false, and `memo('a', {forceRefresh:true})` throws. 'a' is deleted, so membership and calculatedSize change and dispose/disposeAfter fire with reason 'expire'. This violates 'If `memoMethod` throws, `memo()` rethrows that same thrown value without changing cache membership, cached values, recency order, TTL durations or start times, entry sizes, or `calculatedSize`' and 'A `memoMethod` failure causes no `dispose`, `disposeAfter`, or `onInsert` calls attributable to the failed `memo()` operation.' The sealed test misses this because its compound failure forces a refresh of 'b', which is already the most recent entry, with updateAgeOnGet false and the entry not stale. That makes the early #get a no-op. To fix, apply the lookup effects only after memoMethod returns successfully.

The state-changing lookup still runs before the calculation: src/index.ts:3022 contains "this.#get(k, lookupOptions)", followed at :3023 by "const vv = memoMethod(k, v, {".
